Gravitational Wave-Particle Duality

Prior to the 19th Century, it was well-established that light clearly had a wave nature, because it exhibited
wave behaviours such as diffraction and interference during experiments such as Young’s Double Slit
Experiment (1801). On the other hand, matter clearly exhibits a particle nature. This is confirmed, for
example, by the transfer of momentum and energy during collisions between matter particles.

From the early 1900’s, however, some light behaviours were observed that could not be explained solely
by the wave model. One example is the photoelectric effect. (see Figure 1).

Photoelectron ejection is not affected by the intensity of the incident light. It is only observed when the
frequency of the incident light on the metallic surface exceeds a specific minimum frequency. This can
be measured by the circuit shown below which utilises a stopping voltage. This behaviour could not be
explained by the wave model.

Figure 2: Photoelectric Effect Experimental Apparatus

For a metal like Zinc, the following graph (Figure 3) can be generated from the data collected. The
frequency ‘f’ of the incident light is placed on the x-axis; the kinetic energy (Ek) of the ejected
photoelectrons is plotted on the y-axis. The kinetic energy can be determined by the stopping voltage for
each frequency of incident light.

Figure 3: ‘Ek’ v ‘f’ graph

When electrons are passed through a double slit, the same interference pattern is observed as that for
light. This confirms the wave behaviour of mass particles. All objects, therefore, need to be treated as
both/either a wave and/or a particle, depending on the circumstances under consideration. So, what
about gravitational waves?

In February 2016, the detector called LIGO detected gravitational waves for the first time. These waves
had a maximum frequency of 250 Hz. They were formed when two black holes merged (36 solar masses
and 29 solar masses) into one black hole (62 solar masses); and three (3) solar masses was converted
into energy which spread out as gravitational waves travelling at the speed of light.

This event generated a power output of 3.6 × 1049 W – more than the combined power output of all the
observed stars in the Universe. The observed gravitational waves confirmed a vital prediction of
Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity.

If Quantum Physics is right, gravitational waves also possess a wave-particle duality. However, only the
wave nature of gravitational waves has ever been observed - the quantum nature of gravity has not. Just
as water waves are created by vibrating water particles, the Standard Model states that gravitational
waves will consist of vibrating ‘gravitons’ – the quantum particle for gravity.

Light waves consist of oscillating electric and magnetic fields. Gravitational waves cause space itself to
expand and contract in a periodic manner (see Figure 4).

Figure 4: oscillating space in the presence of a gravitational wave.

These waves are expected to propagate through a medium (i.e. – space) at a specific speed (i.e. – the
speed of light ‘c’); interfere with other gravitational waves constructively and destructively; diffract; and,
like light waves, stretch as the Universe expands.

Experiments to find gravitons have, so far, been unsuccessful. Gravitons are thought to be massless and
travel at the speed of light. If they do possess a mass, it is less than 1.6 × 10-22 eV/c2. In addition, they
possess no charge. Until methods for studying gravity at the quantum level are found, finding gravitons
will be very difficult.

One possibility is to use merged black holes. Quantum gravitational effects are strongest and most
pronounced where there are strong gravitational fields in play at very tiny distances. What better tool
could there possibly be to probe this regime than merging black holes? There is still much to learn about
gravitational waves and gravitons. Black holes may hold the key.

html:
Oumuamua – An Interstellar Visitor

On the 19th October, 2017, a team of astronomers viewed a strange object through Hawaii’s Pan-STARR
Telescope hurtling through the Solar System. The astronomers initially thought the object was a comet.
However, after more observations were made, they realised what they had found was more like an
asteroid that had travelled from a stellar system outside the Solar System. The object was named
Oumuamua, a Hawaiian word that translates to “a messenger from afar arriving first”.

Oumuamua did not possess the visible tail typical of a comet. An ordinary comet’s tail is caused by
frozen water and carbon dioxide vaporising as the comet approaches the Sun. This tail can be up to
hundreds of millions of kilometres in length and always points away from the Sun.

In addition, Oumuamua’s path around the Sun differed from that of typical comets in that it seemed to
deviate from one shaped purely by the gravitational force of the Sun. It’s perihelion (i.e. - closest
distance to the Sun) was determined to be 3.84 × 1010 metres (0.256 AU). As it passed around the Sun,
it received a gravitational ‘sling shot’ and picked up speed. At the time it was first observed on 19th
October, Oumuamua was at distance of 2.13 × 1011 metres (1.42 AU) and travelling AWAY from the Sun
with a rapid speed of 87.3 km s-1.

Further measurements of Oumuamua’s velocity revealed an unexpected observation: it was
experiencing a net NON-GRAVITATIONAL accelerating force AWAY from the Sun. This net accelerating
force was calculated to be 4.9 × 10-4 times the gravitational force from the Sun at that distance.
In other words, after experiencing a sling shot and increasing speed, Oumuamua did not seem to be
gravitationally bound to the Sun and was, instead, accelerating outwards as it was leaving the Solar
System.

Given the much lower observed speeds of comets and asteroids originating in the Kuiper Belt within the
Solar System, Oumuamua’s speed precluded it from having originated in the Solar System. This was an
interstellar visitor - and an odd one!

Other telescopes were deployed, and further observations made. Light reflected from Oumuamua
suggested that - at the time of its discovery - it possessed an unexpected ‘rod-shape’. When first
observed, it had estimated dimensions of 45 m × 44 m × 7.5 m. In addition, it appeared to be tumbling
end over end as it accelerated away from the Sun and out of the Solar System.

These unexpected observations (especially the non-gravitational acceleration away from the Sun) led an
astronomer at Harvard University named Avi Loeb to speculate that Oumuamua may be a fully
operational ‘alien probe’ sent to investigate the Earth. He speculated that the acceleration could have
been achieved using ‘solar sail’ technology. This method of propulsion uses ‘radiation pressure’ exerted
by sunlight on large surfaces.

Further observations, however, led to a more ‘natural’ theory to explain Oumuamua’s behaviour. It was
known that collisions with Pluto-like exoplanets in the Kuiper Belt often caused large chunks of nitrogen
(N2) ice to become dislodged and ejected from their surfaces. The presence of similar exoplanets has
been confirmed in other stellar systems orbiting in the Milky Way.

It was determined that the behaviour of Oumuamua could be explained if it was a large chunk of N2 ice
with the dimensions mentioned previously. The estimated mass of the object at the time of discovery
would have been about 8000 tonnes.

This composition would also explain the non-gravitational acceleration observed as being due to a
’recoil’ effect caused by the sublimation of solid N2 ice as Oumuamua absorbed cosmic rays and solar
radiation. The resultant N2 gas is ejected in the opposite direction to Oumuamua’s velocity, causing the
propulsion observed. However, due to Oumuamua’s high speed and low absolute magnitude, a tail was
not able to be seen.

This meant that during its journey through the Solar System, Oumuamua had been losing mass and
volume. Calculations showed that at perihelion, its dimensions would have been 58 m × 56 m × 20 m;
and its mass would have been as high as 95000 tonnes.
